title: Memory Layout: Struct Padding, Field Reordering, #[repr(C)], #[repr(packed)]
prerequisites: Understanding of memory alignment and C ABI

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A parking lot has bays of different widths, and every car must be parked starting at a bay boundary that matches its width (alignment). A small car (1 unit) can park anywhere; a big truck (8 units) must start at an 8-unit boundary. If a lot lists a small car, a truck, and another small car, the truck's boundary rule forces a gap after the first small car — wasted space (padding). Rust by default rearranges the list to minimize gaps; the C-style arrangement keeps your exact order and the gaps that come with it.
progressiveExplaining.junior: Rust structs have a default layout: the compiler can REORDER fields to minimize padding (size = sum of field sizes, rounded up to alignment). The layout is unspecified by default — you can't rely on field order or offsets. #[repr(C)] gives C-compatible layout: fields in declaration order, with C's alignment/padding rules — required for FFI and for matching C structs. #[repr(packed)] removes padding (fields tightly packed) — saves memory but can cause unaligned access (and performance/UB issues on some platforms). #[repr(align(N))] forces a minimum alignment. Use std::mem::size_of and offset_of to check layouts.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, the default Rust layout is the compiler's freedom: rustc (and LLVM) reorder fields to reduce padding while respecting each field's alignment, producing the smallest size for a struct of that shape (the 'optimal' layout, but NOT guaranteed stable). This is why repr(Rust) structs are not FFI-safe. #[repr(C)] pins the layout to the C rules: fields in order, each aligned to its type's alignment, with trailing padding to the struct's alignment. #[repr(packed)] sets all fields to alignment 1 (no padding) — this can make references to fields unaligned, which is UB when dereferenced on strict-alignment architectures (x86 tolerates it, ARM may trap). Choosing the right repr is a memory/FFI/performance trade-off.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: Field placement: each field is placed at an offset that is a multiple of its alignment. Struct alignment = max of field alignments (unless overridden). Default Rust layout runs a packing algorithm (the layout optimizer in rustc/LLVM) that orders fields to pack them; the result is unspecified and can change between versions. #[repr(C)] disables reordering and computes offsets exactly as C does. #[repr(packed)] forces every field to alignment 1, so a u32 field may sit at an odd offset; taking &field creates a reference with the (possibly unaligned) address — the compiler warns, and on strict-alignment targets dereferencing it is UB (use read_unaligned). #[repr(align(N))] raises the struct's alignment (useful for cache-line alignment, SIMD). size_of/align_of report the results.

codeComparison.title: Default repr(Rust) layout vs #[repr(C)]
codeComparison.summary: The default layout reorders fields to pack tightly; #[repr(C)] preserves declaration order with C padding — needed for FFI.

legacyOrBad.label: Assuming field order for FFI
legacyOrBad.snippet: struct Point { x: u8, y: u64, z: u8 } // ❌ OLD: order NOT guaranteed

modernOrGood.label: #[repr(C)] for FFI
modernOrGood.snippet:
#[repr(C)]
struct Point { x: u8, y: u64, z: u8 } // ✅ NEW: C layout, field order fixed

interviewGotchas.question: Why is the default Rust struct layout unspecified, and why does that matter for FFI?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the layout model — interviewers want the field-reordering freedom and why only #[repr(C)] provides the ABI guarantee C code needs.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: The default repr(Rust) layout gives the compiler (rustc + LLVM) the freedom to reorder fields and choose padding to minimize size — an optimization that can change between compiler versions. Because the layout is unspecified and unstable, passing such a struct across an FFI boundary is unsafe: the C side expects a specific layout (declaration order with C alignment/padding), and a reordered Rust struct would be misinterpreted. #[repr(C)] pins the layout to the C rules: exact field order, C alignment, and trailing padding — making the struct ABI-compatible. The same concern applies to serializing structs directly to bytes, reading binary formats, or relying on offset_of for a specific member. If you need a stable layout for any of those, use #[repr(C)] (or repr(packed)/repr(align) as appropriate).
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'struct fields are in declaration order'. Rust's default layout is explicitly unspecified and may reorder. Another trap: thinking size_of alone tells you the layout — two different layouts can have the same size; offsets matter. Candidates who explain the reordering freedom and the FFI guarantee show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: What are the risks of #[repr(packed)], and why does Rust warn about references to packed fields?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This probes the unaligned-access problem — interviewers want the alignment-1 consequence and the UB risk on strict-alignment architectures, plus the safe workaround.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: #[repr(packed)] forces every field to alignment 1 — no padding between fields, giving the smallest possible size. The consequence: fields can sit at unaligned offsets (e.g. a u32 at offset 1). Taking a reference to such a field (&s.field) creates a reference whose address is not aligned to the field's required alignment. On strict-alignment architectures (ARM, and x86 in some SIMD contexts), dereferencing an unaligned reference is undefined behavior — the compiler can miscompile or the CPU can fault. This is why Rust emits a warning when you take a reference to a packed field's member. The safe approach: read/write the field with read_unaligned/write_unaligned (or copy the struct to an aligned location). Use packed layouts deliberately for network/protocol structs and FFI, not casually for 'smaller structs'.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'packed just saves memory, no downside'. It introduces unaligned field access that is UB when dereferenced via a reference on strict-alignment targets. Another trap: thinking x86 makes it always safe — x86 tolerates unaligned loads for most instructions, but the UB contract still lets the optimizer assume alignment, and some operations (atomics, SIMD) fault. Candidates who explain the alignment-1 consequence and read_unaligned show real depth.
